reuse_note: Facts marked reused: true are copied from articles/2026-11-13-marriage-licence-requirements/02-research-A.json (original IDs in use_note), checked 2026-11-13. Nothing applicable was left in marriage-licence-validity/02-research-A.json beyond duplicates of the same AGD facts. FAST mode, one round. AGD Guidelines on the Marriage Act were read from the PDF at ag.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-03/... which is version 4.0 (July 2018); AGD now links a September 2021 edition (ag.gov.au/node/3026) that was not opened, so Guidelines facts are medium unless corroborated by a registry page. Legal confirmations name the authority (celebrant, BDM registry, AGD), never the Wedded Advisor.

facts.claim: Section 44 of the Marriage Act 1961: a marriage shall not be solemnised unless at least 2 persons who are, or appear to the person solemnising the marriage to be, over the age of 18 years are present as witnesses.
facts.publisher: Federal Register of Legislation, Marriage Act 1961 (compilation 9 July 2024)
facts.use_note: Reused from requirements A F-012. 'Appear to the celebrant to be' over 18: the celebrant judges age. The section sets no ID rule for witnesses. Later compilations exist (search showed 2024-10-14 and 2024-12-11); s 44 wording not re-checked against them (N-001).

facts.claim: On the wedding day, 3 marriage certificates must be signed by the couple, the authorised celebrant, and 2 witnesses over 18. The celebrant gives the couple a certificate of marriage on the day, which is a ceremonial certificate. Within 14 days the celebrant submits the paperwork to the BDM registry of the state or territory where the marriage took place.
facts.use_note: Reused from requirements A F-016. Core 'what witnesses sign' fact; names of the 3 certificates in F-016.

facts.claim: Since 12 June 2024 the celebrant must be physically present to solemnise a marriage, together with the parties and 2 witnesses.
facts.use_note: Reused from requirements A F-006. Ceremony witnesses cannot attend by video link. Corroborated by BDM Victoria (F-012): 'A marriage must be solemnised in the physical presence of a celebrant and two witnesses.'

facts.claim: Authorised witnesses for signing the NOIM. In Australia: an authorised celebrant, a justice of the peace, a barrister or solicitor, a medical practitioner, or a member of the Australian Federal Police or a state or territory police force. Outside Australia: an Australian Consular Officer, an Australian Diplomatic Officer, a notary public, or a Commonwealth or Austrade employee authorised under the Consular Fees Act 1955.
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Notice of Intended Marriage form
facts.use_note: Reused from requirements A F-004. Different role from the 2 ceremony witnesses: a NOIM witness is a listed official who identifies you; ceremony witnesses are any 2 people over 18.

facts.claim: Since 12 June 2024 the NOIM may be witnessed in person or remotely by audio-visual link. If the couple is in Australia, the remote witness (which can be a celebrant) must also be in Australia; if the couple is outside Australia, the authorised witness (who cannot be a celebrant) must also be outside Australia. You cannot witness online a NOIM for a person or couple outside Australia.
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Notice of Intended Marriage
facts.use_note: Reused from requirements A F-005. Video-link scope is NOIM witnessing only, never the ceremony (F-003). Older AGD Guidelines (2018) said NOIMs could not be witnessed over Skype; superseded by the 2024 amendment.

facts.claim: Vows (section 45(2)): where the celebrant is not a minister of religion, each party says to the other, in the presence of the celebrant and the witnesses: 'I call upon the persons here present to witness that I, A.B. (or C.D.), take thee, C.D. (or A.B.), to be my lawful wedded wife (or husband, or spouse)' or words to that effect. The monitum (s 46) is also said 'in the presence of these witnesses'.
facts.publisher: Federal Register of Legislation, Marriage Act 1961 (compilation 9 July 2024)
facts.use_note: Reused from requirements A F-013 and F-014 (medium on the 'not a minister of religion' scope). Shows why witnesses must be present for the legal words. Guidelines (2018) allow 'these witnesses' in the monitum to become 'everyone here' but not 'family and friends'.

facts.claim: NSW Government (BDM): you are legally required to have 2 witnesses at your ceremony to witness and sign the marriage certificate. If possible you should know the witnesses, as their evidence can be used to establish the identity of the couple and testify to the circumstances in which the ceremony was performed. Witnesses need to be 18 years or older and speak and understand English. During the ceremony you, your celebrant and your witnesses sign two official certificates of marriage and one ceremonial certificate.
facts.publisher: NSW Government, Getting married in NSW (Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages)
facts.use_note: Sydney market. 'Speak and understand English' is registry guidance, not in s 44; see F-009 and F-010 on interpreters.

facts.claim: AGD Guidelines on the Marriage Act (Part 5.8 Witnesses): the 2 witnesses sign the marriage certificates in their capacity as witnesses and should record their names in full, including any middle names. Their evidence is available to establish the identity of the parties or testify to the circumstances of the ceremony, so it is best practice (but not a requirement of the Marriage Act) that the witnesses know the parties. Arranging witnesses is the couple's responsibility; the celebrant is not responsible for providing them.
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Guidelines on the Marriage Act 1961 for authorised celebrants (version 4.0, July 2018)
facts.use_note: Medium only because the September 2021 edition was not opened (N-002). The 'know the witnesses' purpose is corroborated by NSW (F-007, high). Answers 'can a stranger be a witness': legally yes, best practice no.

facts.claim: AGD Guidelines (Part 5.9 Interpreters): under section 112 of the Marriage Act a celebrant may use an interpreter where they consider it desirable; it is prudent when any one of the celebrant, the parties or the witnesses does not understand the language of the ceremony, including sign language such as Auslan. The interpreter must not be a party to the marriage. The celebrant must receive the interpreter's statutory declaration (that they understand and can converse in the languages) before solemnising, and immediately after the ceremony the interpreter gives a certificate of faithful performance in the approved form. The celebrant decides whether an interpreter is needed.
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Guidelines on the Marriage Act 1961 for authorised celebrants (version 4.0, July 2018)
facts.use_note: Witnesses must understand the language of the ceremony or an interpreter is used; the celebrant decides. s 112 text not read on legislation.gov.au (N-001).

facts.claim: Witness as interpreter. AGD Guidelines 5.9.1: the Marriage Act does not prohibit an interpreter and a witness being the same person, but it is recommended the interpreter's professionalism is not compromised by also being a witness. Queensland's Brisbane Registry: an interpreter can be a certified (NAATI) interpreter or someone who speaks both languages and is not one of the people getting married or one of the witnesses.
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Guidelines (v4.0 July 2018); Queensland Government, Brisbane Registry What to bring
facts.use_note: Sources differ: AGD says legal but not recommended; the Brisbane Registry excludes witnesses as interpreters for its own ceremonies (https://www.qld.gov.au/family/marriage-and-civil-partnerships/brisbane-registry-weddings/the-brisbane-registry/on-the-day-accordion/what-to-bring , updated 2 April 2025). Write: 'Choose an interpreter who is not one of your two witnesses; your celebrant decides.'

facts.claim: Queensland Government (Brisbane Registry weddings): you must have at least 2 guests to witness the ceremony and sign the marriage certificate. Witnesses can be family or friends and do not need to be Australian citizens. They need to be 18 or older, speak and understand English, and be at the entire ceremony. The Registry cannot supply witnesses.
facts.publisher: Queensland Government, Brisbane Registry weddings, What to bring
facts.use_note: Brisbane market. These are Registry ceremony rules; 'not citizens' and 'whole ceremony' are useful general guidance for destination guests.

facts.claim: BDM Victoria: you cannot get married online; a marriage must be solemnised in the physical presence of a celebrant and two witnesses. You need two witnesses at your wedding ceremony to witness the ceremony and sign the marriage certificates. Witnesses can be any family member or friend who is at least 18 years old.
facts.publisher: Births, Deaths and Marriages Victoria, Getting married in Victoria
facts.use_note: Melbourne market. Best official answer to 'can family be witnesses': yes, any family member, which covers parents, siblings and a partner's relatives.

facts.claim: AGD Guidelines 6.8.1 and 6.8.2: no one other than the 2 witnesses may add a signature to the couple's (Form 15) certificate of marriage; the two witnesses are the official legal witnesses and their presence serves a legal purpose (to swear in court or elsewhere to the identity of the parties and the circumstances, date and place of the ceremony). Children of one or both parties who are under 18 cannot sign the certificate; if over 18 and acting as one of the two witnesses, they may sign in that capacity.
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Guidelines on the Marriage Act 1961 for authorised celebrants (version 4.0, July 2018)
facts.use_note: Answers 'can our children be witnesses': yes if 18 or over. No guest-signing on the legal certificate; suggest a separate guest book. Medium pending the 2021 edition (N-002).

facts.claim: AGD Guidelines 11.6 and 11.7: celebrants may conduct commitment ceremonies, which are not marriages and must not purport to be one. The celebrant must not prepare or submit any paperwork (such as the NOIM and declarations as to conjugal status). Witnesses are not required for a commitment ceremony. A certificate of marriage, or any certificate referring to the Marriage Act, must not be prepared, and celebrants should avoid the words 'wedding' or 'marriage'. The same applies to renewal of vows ceremonies.
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Guidelines on the Marriage Act 1961 for authorised celebrants (version 4.0, July 2018)
facts.use_note: Direct official answer: a symbolic or commitment ceremony needs no legal witnesses. Couples marrying abroad with a symbolic ceremony still need the legal witnesses at the legal step (destination rules belong to batch B).

facts.claim: The three certificates are: the Official Certificate of Marriage (celebrant copy), the Official Certificate of Marriage on the back of the Declaration of No Legal Impediment to Marriage (BDM copy, forwarded to the registry), and the Form 15 Certificate of Marriage given to the couple immediately after the ceremony. The celebrant keeps the celebrant copy for six years.
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Your responsibilities as a marriage celebrant
facts.use_note: Names what the witnesses sign. Pair with F-002.

facts.claim: If an error on the marriage certificates is found after the ceremony, the celebrant may correct it only while the parties and witnesses are still present (initialled by the celebrant, with a covering note to the BDM). Once they have left, the celebrant cannot correct it; after registration only the BDM registry's authorised officer can (s 51 of the Act).
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Your responsibilities as a marriage celebrant
facts.use_note: Practical tip: witnesses should check names and spelling before leaving the signing table.

facts.claim: NSW Government NOIM guidance: the NOIM witness must watch you sign and date the notice, then write their full name and their qualification as an authorised witness (for example a JP number, or a police officer's station) and sign. The witness is declaring that they have identified you as the parties wanting to marry. A pharmacist, psychologist, nurse, physiotherapist or dentist does not qualify as a NOIM witness.
facts.publisher: NSW Government, Getting married in NSW (NOIM video transcript)
facts.use_note: Contrasts NOIM witness (identifies you, must hold a listed qualification) with ceremony witnesses (any 2 adults). Pair with F-004 and F-005.

legal.summary: At least 2 witnesses who are, or appear to the celebrant to be, over 18 must be present (Marriage Act s 44). Confirmed by AGD (Get married page) and NSW, VIC and QLD BDM registries; your celebrant confirms on the day.
Couple, celebrant and both witnesses sign 3 marriage certificates; celebrant lodges with the state or territory BDM within 14 days. Confirmed by AGD.
Celebrant, couple and 2 witnesses must be physically present; no video-link ceremonies. Confirmed by AGD and BDM Victoria.

NOIM witnesses are listed officials (JP, lawyer, doctor, police, celebrant in Australia; consular officer or notary public abroad), a different role from ceremony witnesses. Confirmed by AGD (NOIM form) and NSW BDM.
Remote NOIM witnessing since 12 June 2024 (witness in the same country as the couple; no online witnessing for a couple outside Australia). Confirmed by AGD.

Interpreter under s 112 when a party or witness does not understand the ceremony language; statutory declaration before, certificate of faithful performance after. The celebrant decides; AGD Guidelines confirm.
Witnesses can be any family member or friend aged 18 or over. Confirmed by BDM Victoria; QLD Registry says family or friends, citizenship not required.
Couple's children may witness only if 18 or over; no extra signatures on the certificate. AGD Guidelines confirm (2018 edition; your celebrant confirms current practice).
Commitment and vow renewal ceremonies are not marriages; no NOIM, no certificate, witnesses not required. AGD Guidelines confirm.

needs.need: Re-read Marriage Act ss 44 and 112 in the latest compilation on legislation.gov.au (later compilations than 9 July 2024 exist). FAST mode did not open them.

Open the current AGD Guidelines on the Marriage Act (September 2021 edition, https://www.ag.gov.au/node/3026) to confirm Parts 5.8, 5.9, 6.8 and 11.6 are unchanged from the 2018 version read (F-008, F-009, F-010, F-013, F-014). Upgrade to high if unchanged.

Can the celebrant also be one of the two witnesses? No official source found either way. The registries treat the celebrant and the 2 witnesses as separate people (VIC 'physical presence of a celebrant and two witnesses'). Do not state a rule; write 'plan on two people besides your celebrant' and have the couple's celebrant confirm.

ID requirements for ceremony witnesses: no official source sets any. s 44 says witnesses must be, or appear to the celebrant to be, over 18; NSW and AGD ask for full names. Whether celebrants may ask witnesses for ID is celebrant practice, not sourced.

Conflict to flag: NSW and QLD registries say witnesses must 'speak and understand English', while AGD Guidelines contemplate an interpreter where a witness does not understand the ceremony language. Treat English as registry guidance; the celebrant decides under s 112. Celebrant confirmation advised.

No official source addresses whether a witness may be a relative of a party beyond VIC 'any family member' and QLD 'family or friends' (no restriction found). Nothing found restricting a partner's relative.
Witness rules abroad (Italy, Greece, France, Bali, Fiji): batch B scope, not covered here.
Real client stories (choosing witnesses, a witness who was a child of the couple, using an interpreter at a destination wedding): business input only.
